Lessons.Title: Make Sense of Data
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: read picture graphs and bar graphs with one-unit scales, describe what their data show and invent questions answerable from those displays. This is Grade 3, Unit 1, Lesson 1 of the 2021 first-edition curriculum; drawings and wording are independently authored by Edulytics.

Warm-up (15 minutes): before naming a context, study six upright picture-graph columns with 4, 3, 1, 2, 7 and 6 symbols from left to right. Each symbol represents one student. The category labels are not supplied, so their names cannot be inferred as facts. Think quietly, then explain one observation and one genuine question with a partner. The teacher records ideas and opens Math Community discussion. The 2021 teacher warm-up gives 1 minute of individual quiet time, 1 minute of partner discussion, and then introduces the Students/Teacher by Doing Math/Norms Math Community T-chart in warm-up synthesis.

Activity 1 — Picture Time (10 minutes): reveal the title 'How We Get Home' but NOT the category labels. Discuss possible ways children travel home and justify why these are plausible possibilities rather than proven category names. The same column heights and one-student key remain unchanged. Activity 1 begins with 30 seconds to notice the added graph title, followed by 2–3 minutes of partner reasoning about plausible unlabeled categories.

Activity 2 — Picture Graphs and Bar Graphs (20 minutes): reveal the actual labels and counts: Walk 4, Bike 3, Skateboard 1, Car 2, Bus 7, Train 6. Show the identical dataset in a six-column one-symbol-per-student picture graph and a bar graph with a vertical scale 0 through 8 in increments of 1 and horizontal axis 'Ways to get home'. First compare the two displays, next explain what they teach us about the data, then write two distinct graph questions that can be answered from the visible values. Partner reasoning, written comparisons and learner-authored questions require teacher evaluation, not a numeric pass. Activity 2 includes 2 minutes of partner graph comparison, then 7–10 minutes for the three distinct source questions and MLR8 partner restatement.

Lesson synthesis (10 minutes): summarize the role of the graph title, category labels, picture key and bar-number scale. Ask students to restate a peer's justified observation, and reflect on mathematical participation and class norms. Follow with a separate 5-minute Edulytics-authored independent Cool-down about a fictional library survey; this checks the same graph-reading skills but is NOT the unavailable publisher Cool-down. A public 2021 first-edition Grade 3 Unit 1 teacher-guide extract now confirms that the source Cool-down asks for TWO separate human-judged products: one graph-supported fact and one new answerable question. The original teacher-guide graphic is a separate four-category travel bar chart (bike, walk, bus, car), NOT the six-category lesson graph. The independent Edulytics library survey practices those two types without claiming identical publisher data, rights or teacher marking.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unlabelled categories
KeyConcepts.Definition: A column without its category label shows a quantity but does not identify what the category means.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use shown counts for observations; describe proposed categories as guesses until labelled.
KeyConcepts.Example: The first untitled picture graph has heights 4, 3, 1, 2, 7 and 6; 'bus' is not yet a verified label.

KeyConcepts.Title: Picture-graph key
KeyConcepts.Definition: A picture graph displays data with repeated symbols, interpreted using its key.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Here exactly one symbol means one student; count individual symbols within each category.
KeyConcepts.Example: After labels are revealed, Bus has 7 symbols, so 7 students take the bus.

KeyConcepts.Title: Bar-graph scale and categories
KeyConcepts.Definition: A bar graph represents each category's count as a bar height against a number axis.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Here bars start at zero; the vertical axis is 0 to 8 in steps of 1 and the horizontal axis describes ways to get home.
KeyConcepts.Example: The Train bar reaches 6 and the Skateboard bar reaches 1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Answerable data questions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A question is answerable when its requested fact follows from the categories and their counts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check both which categories are identified and which values are displayed before answering; explanations remain teacher-reviewed.
KeyConcepts.Example: 'How many more take the bus than skateboard?' is answerable: 7 − 1 = 6. 'Why do they take the bus?' is not answered by the graph.

WorkedExamples.Title: Warm-up — notice before labelling
WorkedExamples.Question: An untitled picture graph has six anonymous columns of 4, 3, 1, 2, 7 and 6 unit symbols. What can you say with certainty?
WorkedExamples.Method: Separate observed quantities from guessed category names. This is an illustrative open response, not a fixed-response original-source answer.
Steps: Read the key: one picture stands for one student.
Count the first and fifth columns: 4 and 7, respectively.
Observe that the fifth anonymous column has three more symbols than the first: 7 − 4 = 3.
Do not assign a definite travel label before the source reveals one; offer a question to discuss with a partner.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The fifth unknown category has 7 students; it has 3 more than the first unknown category. Category names remain unknown.
WorkedExamples.Check: Quantities and comparison follow from 7 − 4 = 3. A teacher reviews the observation and the learner's question.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 1 — distinguish context from label
WorkedExamples.Question: The title 'How We Get Home' is added to the same anonymous columns. Can we now prove which column means walking?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the title only as context; an explanation needs human review.
Steps: Read the title to identify the kind of information represented.
Notice that no individual column names have been supplied.
Suggest walking, cycling or travelling by bus as possible ways home.
Explain why the title alone does not associate any possibility with a particular column.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No. The title concerns travel home, but without category labels no specific column can be identified as walking.
WorkedExamples.Check: The graph's six heights and one-student key have not changed; no known category-to-column association exists.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 2 — interpret and compare both graphs
WorkedExamples.Question: The revealed labels are Walk 4, Bike 3, Skateboard 1, Car 2, Bus 7 and Train 6. Give one comparison and two distinct answerable questions.
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the unit-key picture graph and the zero-aligned one-unit bar graph as two representations of the SAME survey; questions and reasoning require teacher review.
Steps: Match all six names and quantities in both displays in the original order.
Verify each picture counts one student, each bar starts at zero and the numbered vertical axis increments by one.
Compare Bus 7 and Skateboard 1 to get a difference of 6.
Check two different questions: 'How many take the bus?' and 'How many travel by bus or train?'
WorkedExamples.Answer: Bus has 6 more students than Skateboard; 7 students take the bus; 13 students take bus or train.
WorkedExamples.Check: 7 − 1 = 6 and 7 + 6 = 13. A teacher additionally evaluates each source graph comparison and original learner-authored questions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assigning a known travel method to an anonymous column in the warm-up or Picture Time.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The bars show counts, but a title does not disclose the mapping from those counts to categories.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record the observation as a count and describe a travel label only as a suggestion until the labelled graph appears.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Counting one picture as several students or treating the bar-number axis as a two-unit scale.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The published 2021 task has key one symbol = one student and bar ticks 0 through 8 by one.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Confirm the key and use one-unit steps on a zero-aligned axis; each bar height equals its category count.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Substituting a correct numeric response for comparing two graph forms or writing questions.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The first-edition Student Facing activity includes three open parts about similarities, information and two questions, none of which is established by a single number.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep the five original Student Facing subparts separate in the companion and require human rubric review.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting an independent assessment or artwork as the publisher's original.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The publisher's educator-only Cool-down and exact image asset are not confirmed and must not be misrepresented.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Mark the library-survey Cool-down as Edulytics-authored and provide attribution and rights boundaries.

SummaryPoints: 15-minute Warm-up: six anonymous picture columns 4, 3, 1, 2, 7 and 6, one student per symbol; notice and wonder with a partner.
10-minute Picture Time: the title How We Get Home gives context but leaves category names unknown.
20-minute Activity 2: Walk 4, Bike 3, Skateboard 1, Car 2, Bus 7, Train 6 in BOTH a picture graph and 0–8, one-unit vertical bar graph.
Five distinct source Student Facing subparts require teacher review: notice/wonder; possible categories; compare graph types; explain information; write two answerable questions.
Finish 10-minute synthesis and Math Community reflection before the separate five-minute independent Edulytics Cool-down; do not claim publisher Cool-down or artwork parity.

The public 2021 three-page Student Task Statements PDF was read directly: warm-up Notice and Wonder, 1.1 Picture Time, and 1.2 Picture Graphs and Bar Graphs with three parts. These five original Student Facing requests retain separate teacher-reviewed responses.

2021 Cool-down skill types independently confirmed from public first-edition Teacher Guide: one graph fact plus one answerable question, both open teacher-review tasks; the original bar-graph picture and publisher-item identity are not reused.
